# You Are Buying Media and You Do Not Trust the Numbers. You Are Right Not To.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Programmatic reports are built to be legible, not true. The ANA found only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer, so the reported CPM understates the price of impressions that could have mattered. This playbook sets out how to calculate a real CPM, why the rejection rate is the number to watch, and six questions to ask before the next invoice.

The programmatic report arrives on the first of the month, and it is beautiful: impressions in the tens of millions, a CPM lower than last quarter's, a cost per click that seems too good. If you have wondered what any of that actually bought, you are not being paranoid. The ANA found that only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer. The reporting layer of programmatic advertising was designed to be legible, not to be true. The fix is to report a different set of numbers: real CPM, verification pass rate and rejection rate.

## Impressions are the least informative number on the page

An impression is a record that an ad was served. It says nothing about whether a human was present, whether the page had any reason to exist beyond hosting ads, or whether the placement was one the company would ever have chosen on purpose.

The Association of National Advertisers' 2023 study of programmatic supply chains analysed 35.5 billion impressions from 21 advertisers. It found that made-for-advertising (MFA) sites, pages built to be filled with ads and visited by arbitraged traffic, took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend. The average campaign ran across more than 40,000 websites. Those impressions are cheap. They lower the average CPM. They also do nothing.

A low CPM, in other words, can be a symptom rather than a result.

Viewability is better than an impression count, but it is a floor rather than a measure of value. The Media Rating Council's standard counts a display ad as viewable when 50% of its pixels are on screen for one continuous second, and a video ad for two. A viewability rate in the high sixties means roughly a third of what was paid for did not meet even that bar.

## What a real CPM is

Take the media cost. Remove the impressions that failed verification: invalid traffic, out-of-geography, non-viewable, made-for-advertising placements, and any inventory outside the company's own inclusion list. Divide the money by what is left, and multiply by a thousand.

| Line | Impressions | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Served and reported | 20,000,000 | Reported CPM on $50,000 spend: $2.50 |
| Less invalid traffic | 600,000 | Bots and automated traffic caught by verification |
| Less non-viewable | 6,000,000 | Failed the MRC viewability standard |
| Less MFA placements | 2,400,000 | Sites built to host ads |
| Less out-of-geo and off inclusion list | 1,000,000 | Outside the buyer's own rules |
| Impressions that could have mattered | 10,000,000 | Real CPM: $5.00 |

*Illustrative figures, assuming no overlap between categories.*

That number is the real CPM, and it is often two to three times the reported one. The ANA's figures support the range: if only 36 cents of a dollar reaches a consumer, the effective price of a useful impression is nearly three times the headline. Its quarterly benchmark, built with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia, found that in the fourth quarter of 2025 the stronger advertisers had 56.7% of programmatic spend meet its quality criteria (fraud-free, measurable, viewable and MFA-free), against 37.5% for the weaker ones. That is a multiple of about 1.8 for the first group and 2.7 for the second.

It is the only CPM worth comparing across partners, months or channels, because it is the price of impressions that could conceivably have mattered. A desk that cannot produce this figure is reporting the price of a bag of impressions without opening the bag. The ANA benchmark also reported advertiser cases in which cost per conversion fell by nearly 40% after optimising on quality-adjusted measures instead of CPM, even though nominal CPMs rose.

> Reported CPM, impressions and viewability describe a bag of inventory. Real CPM, verification and rejection rate describe what was inside it.

## Rejection rate is the number to watch

The most useful single figure in programmatic is the rejection rate: the share of bid opportunities or served impressions the buy declined or discarded because they failed the company's standards.

A high rejection rate is not a problem. It is evidence that someone is choosing. A buy with a rejection rate near zero is accepting whatever the exchanges offer, and the exchanges offer what is cheapest to fill. The ANA's advice to rely on inclusion lists rather than exclusion lists, which it called "largely ineffective" because new domains appear daily, is in practice advice to reject more.

Ask for the rejection rate by partner and by reason. Then ask what the standards were. If nobody can answer the second question, there were no standards.

## Six questions before the next invoice

| Question | What a good answer looks like |
| --- | --- |
| What share of impressions passed verification, and what did the rest fail on? | A pass rate by partner, with failures split into invalid traffic, viewability, geography, MFA and brand safety |
| Which domains and apps received the most spend, and would we have chosen them ourselves? | A top-50 placement list the marketing lead can read and defend |
| What is the real CPM, after removing everything that failed? | A single figure, calculated the same way every month |
| What is the rejection rate, and what rules produced it? | A rate by partner and reason, and the written standard behind it |
| Which fees sit between our budget and the publisher, and what share of the dollar arrives? | A fee per layer, from log-level data the contract gives you access to |
| Which outcomes, not clicks, can the buy be connected to, using tracking we control? | Leads, applications or sales matched in your own systems, ideally with a holdout |

None of these is hostile. A competent desk will have the answers before you ask. A dashboard will not. The last question deserves the most weight: our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to design a holdout at volumes a mid-size buyer can afford, and [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) sets out why a measure must reconcile to finance before anyone acts on it.

## Why the fee structure decides the answers

Media bought on a percentage of spend rewards spending. Every incentive in that arrangement points toward more impressions at a lower average price, which is exactly the recipe for made-for-advertising inventory and a rejection rate of zero. The ANA's study, which found transaction costs absorbed about 29% of each dollar, recommended that advertisers hold direct contracts with each link in the chain and secure access to log-level data. Both are easier when the desk has no reason to resist them.

A flat fee per account changes the question the desk is answering. It stops being "how much can we place?" and becomes "did it work, and can we show it?" That is also why a desk should never front the media spend: the moment the desk is a lender, its interest in the volume of spend returns through the back door. Our piece on [percentage-of-spend media fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) sets out the alternatives in detail.

The numbers can be trusted. They just have to be the right numbers, produced by someone with no reason to flatter them.

Illustrative example: changing the report before changing the buy

Decision
:   Replace the monthly programmatic report's headline CPM with a real CPM, a verification pass rate by partner and a rejection rate by reason, before changing any targeting.

Reason and owner
:   The marketing lead could not reconcile a falling CPM with flat lead volume. Owned by the head of marketing, with the desk producing the figures.

What changed
:   The first real CPM was a little over twice the reported one. Two partners with the lowest reported CPMs had the highest real CPMs and were cut; the remaining budget moved to an inclusion list of about 300 domains.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consumer finance advertiser, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Distrust the headline CPM.** It is lowered by the impressions least likely to matter.
- **Calculate the real CPM.** Media cost divided by impressions that passed verification and your own rules.
- **Read the rejection rate.** Near zero means nobody is choosing.
- **Ask the six questions.** A competent desk has the answers ready.
- **Check the fee.** A percentage of spend pays the desk to accept volume.
